## TL;DR

Engineering and review report histories now present rounds and passes with the same newest-first ordering, compact local timestamps, and an accessible styled disclosure for the full timestamp. The engineering table is left aligned, matching the Review table. A capture fixture seeds six engineering rounds for the declared Dev report shot. The required scoped RepoOS check passed.

## Work and rationale

The report history tables were already using a shared table class, but its base cell rule aligned every column to the right. Review compensated with per-cell left alignment classes while Engineering did not, which made the styles appear inconsistent and left Engineering with right-aligned headers. I changed the shared table rule to left alignment and kept the existing shared row class and selection behavior. This applies a consistent base treatment to both tables and removes the engineering-only alignment mismatch.

Review history already derives rows in descending pass order. Engineering reports came directly from the server response, so the table reflected that response’s ascending order. I added a computed display list that sorts by round descending without mutating the fetched array. The report selection still uses round identity, so clicking or keyboard-activating a displayed row selects the matching report regardless of its position in the source list. The focused component test verifies that the newest round is first, the oldest is last, and keyboard selection follows the reordered rows.

The time helpers live in `src/ui-app/src/lib/time.ts`, so I added two reusable helpers there. The compact helper returns only the local clock time when a timestamp is on today’s local calendar date; otherwise it prepends the locale’s short numeric month/day date. Comparing local year, month, and day avoids treating a timestamp as “today” solely because it is within the last 24 hours. The full helper formats local year, abbreviated month, day, and clock time including seconds. Both return an empty string for missing or invalid values, following the existing time helper conventions.

Both report tables now render the same native `details` and `summary` structure around the compact timestamp, with the full value in a `role="tooltip"` element. The structure is keyboard focusable and opens on activation, and CSS also reveals the styled popup on hover and focus. Native disclosure behavior supplies touch activation without extra JavaScript. The shared CSS provides its focus ring and popup styling; there is no native `title` tooltip. The existing row remains independently selectable.

## Approaches tried

I retained the report tables’ existing row model and common table class rather than introducing a separate component for a small shared timestamp cell. A computed descending list proved sufficient for engineering ordering, while keeping the API response intact for report selection and refresh logic. For the popup, I chose the browser’s disclosure element with custom styling. This provides a compact, keyboard- and touch-usable interaction without a new dependency or a bespoke event state machine.

The first focused run found an existing fixture test whose catch-all branch assumed every new fixture was a failed-check drawer. I made the new engineering fixture explicit in that test and reran it successfully. No production implementation adjustment was needed for that failure.

## Challenges and blockers

The full scoped check took longer than the local UI build because RepoOS sent the changed-path suite to its configured remote runner. The remote validation completed successfully: the build passed, all 5,071 tests passed with one skipped, and the UI smoke and rendered contrast gates passed. The local check then repeated its rendered contrast audit, which took about two and a half minutes, and completed successfully along with local format, lint, build, and UI smoke. No blocking issue remains.

The declared screenshot needs a stable engineering history even though the fixture task has no server-side report records. I added a preview-only fixture state that seeds the fake task and returns six local display rows only while the capture URL is active. The shot targets task 9999, selects the Dev Report pane, and highlights the fixture card, keeping its selector scoped to one task card.

## Key learnings

A shared class does not guarantee consistent table alignment when a subset of cells carries explicit overrides. Aligning the shared table baseline makes future rows consistent and reduces the need for column-specific alignment patches. Similarly, sorting only the display projection is safer than changing source data when selection and refresh logic depend on the original collection.

Local date labeling should use calendar boundaries in the user’s timezone. Elapsed-time tests can mislabel a timestamp around midnight, while a local year/month/day comparison matches what the date portion communicates. The test uses the injected `now` value and checks output through the same locale APIs as the implementation, so it stays deterministic across timezone and locale settings.

Finally, a disclosure element is a useful fit for short metadata with optional detail: it provides an actionable focus target, touch activation, and expanded content semantics using native behavior, while the shared stylesheet gives it the product’s visual treatment.
